13.0.s.en: (1) The service of love and the washing of the feet

13.0.0.en: This refers to Thursday evening, when the Lord knew, by His divinity, that the time of His betrayal had come. Note the contrast with what St. John mentioned earlier, and repeatedly: every time the Jews tried to seize Jesus they did not succeed, although He was in their midst, because His hour had not yet come. Here, however, he declares to us that Christ knew the appointed time, and prepares us for the last stage of Christ's life on earth. He also used the word "departure" instead of the word "death," as a new theological expression that clarifies the nature of bodily death in the understanding of the children of God: it is a passing from one life to another life. This is what the Church uses in her prayers, when she says: "There is no death for Your servants, but a departure." St. John concludes his words by revealing the secret behind what Christ was about to undertake of suffering, torment and crucifixion: His eternal and boundless love for His creation, which He was about to redeem.

13.0.1.en: We may note that St. John is the one who spoke most about divine love, as though he were the disciple who knew the heart of Christ best. This is true, for his gentle nature made him cling more closely to the Lord Jesus, so he was more aware of His love and better able to express it.

13.0.2.en: The invitation is to all of us, to enjoy this overflowing love, which is available to each one of us if he wishes.

13.1.0.en: That is, at the time of the Jewish Passover supper, and before it was completed.

13.1.1.en: "The devil having now put": this shows us the role of Satan in provoking and inciting the carrying out of evil; but he chose the weak soul that would respond to his counsel. He tries with everyone, but the human will is responsible for falling or for resisting. Perhaps St. John pictures for us that one table held both the heart of God, who loves to the end, and the heart of the wicked man who was about to betray Him.

13.2.0.en: St. John repeats the word "knowing" as clear and strong indications of the divinity of Christ. The expression "the Father had given all things into His hands" has two meanings:

13.2.1.en: The first: the complete authority of Christ, which is entirely heavenly, the authority of the Father.

13.2.2.en: The second: a preparation for what the God was about to do.

13.2.3.en: For with these very two hands, into which all the authority of the Father was given, the Lord was going to bend down and wash the feet of the disciples.

13.2.4.en: "He was come from God": that is, by His incarnation, in which He emptied Himself and hid His glory. But His coming forth does not mean that He left Him, for He is united with Him in divinity.

13.2.5.en: "And went to God": that is, the return to His glory in the bosom of the Father. But He will not leave us either, because of His work and care for us, even though He will be hidden from our eyes in His body.

13.3.0.en: He rose after supper was prepared and before beginning to eat it, took the form of a servant ready for a lowly task, humbly laid aside His garments and girded Himself with a towel, in order to undertake a work that no man could understand or mind comprehend ... that is, to begin to wash the feet of His disciples, a work that the ordinary human soul rejects. The dust on the feet is a symbol of sins, and washing them with water points to Baptism and repentance, and this by the hand of Christ, which was to be crucified on the Cross and redeem man.

13.4.0.en: Christ may have begun to wash the feet of the disciples, who were seized with amazement and made no comment, until He came to Peter; or He may have begun with Peter, as St. Augustine thought, and Peter expressed his astonishment and his rejection of the idea, voicing it in a question of protest: Do You, my righteous Lord, wash the feet of a sinner like me?! This reminds us of the attitude of the Baptist, when he held back from baptizing the Savior when He came to him. But Christ's answer, in both cases, contained insistence and decisiveness, not without gentleness, in order to accomplish His purpose. For what Christ wanted by the washing of the feet Peter did not understand at that time ... But what was it that he did not understand?

13.4.1.en: The first lesson: humility. If the Lord of the whole world, its Teacher, Creator and Redeemer, bent down to wash the filth of others in true humility, correcting the concept of authority in the minds of all people, how much more ought we to do likewise with others.

13.4.2.en: The second lesson: not condemning. Removing the filth means helping a person to be rid of sin, by our having a positive work with him, and not being content with pointing at his uncleanness, as the Jews did with the woman caught in adultery (ch. 8:1-11).

13.4.3.en: Because of the greatness of what the Lord Christ did with all humanity in the person of His disciples, the Church arranged in her prayers the rite of the Lakkan of Holy Thursday, by which she recalls all these lessons to our minds. The priest, or the bishop, or the Patriarch stands and girds himself with a towel, in imitation of his Lord, and begins to wash the feet of the deacons and the people, and the rest of the priests help him in the same work. So we remember what the Lord did for us, and we also understand that God appointed bishops and priests as shepherds and servants, first of all for the service of His people and their repentance.

13.5.0.en: Although the virtue of Peter's humility and his shyness appeared in this refusal, it was misplaced, because he did not grasp the spiritual meaning. Therefore Christ made clear to Peter that what He was doing was not an optional work in which Peter had the right to accept or refuse, but that everything depended on it. For this washing is a symbol of the cleansing that comes by the blood of Christ, and whoever refuses has no part with Christ Himself; that is, there is no salvation outside the blood of Christ.

13.6.0.en: Peter was taken aback by Christ's answer, and could only ask for even more, that the washing include his whole body, declaring that he did not want a single thing to separate him from Christ.

13.7.0.en: "He that is washed": this means the washing of Baptism, built on faith in the power of the blood of Christ to cleanse from all sins. Whoever has been washed does not need to be washed again, that is, to repeat Baptism, but needs only to wash his feet ... This is also what the Church teaches her children: the sacrament of Baptism is not repeated, even if a person leaves the faith and returns to it again ... But the washing of the feet, that is, the sacrament of repentance and confession, a person needs always, for the feet are a symbol of the soul that lives in the world and moves about in it, and so becomes soiled with many sins, and is always in need of the washing of repentance.

13.7.1.en: The Lord Christ, by His foreknowledge, adds a hidden allusion to Judas, who would betray Him, since He declared all the disciples clean except one.

13.8.0.en: "Know ye": without doubt, what the Lord had done was far beyond the disciples' imagining? And had it not been for the Lord's decisive word to Peter, they would not have allowed Him to wash their feet. So Christ used the form of a question as an introduction to a teaching discourse.

13.9.0.en: This completes that introduction in establishing the truth that He is the true Lord and Teacher, who must be respected and honored.

13.10.0.en: Here comes the essence of the teaching about what the Lord Jesus did. If the Lord and Teacher did this, how much more should the servant do for his brother ... If the servant does this for his brother, it is not counted to him as a boast, but is only an imitation of the greatest Teacher. And whoever among us considers himself a lord and teacher and not a servant, let him also bend down, overcome by Christ's love for him and His wonderful humility in washing the feet of all. The washing here is not literal, but carries in its meaning all the Christian virtues: endurance, self-giving and self-denial. And when Christ says: "ye also ought," this became an obligation for us and not a choice or a favor from us; that is, it is a commandment that must be carried out, but it requires of all of us self-emptying and true contrition.

13.11.0.en: The Lord affirms once more that, since the servant is not greater than his lord, he must not be ashamed or disdain to do what the Lord did. The Lord Christ also declares the distinction between the one who sends and the one sent, in a clear reference to the work of ministry in His Church: He is the Sender who calls the servant to His service, so the servant must imitate the humility of Him who sent him in his ministry, bearing with those he serves and being patient with them.

13.11.1.en: Christ concludes His teaching here by clarifying the difference between a person's understanding and grasping something and his carrying it out in his life. For the reward and the crown here are counted, not to the one who knows the commandment from his youth (Mt 19:20), but to the one who strives against himself in order to live by it.

13.12.0.en: There is no exception for Judas from the sending, nor from the application to him of all the preceding words (v. 10). He adds that although the Lord chose Judas, for the call is to all, Judas chose betrayal by his own will. Christ points to a scriptural witness, which is what came in Psalm 41:9: "Mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me," in that what David said about the betrayal of Ahithophel is also a prophecy about Judas' betrayal of Christ. The meaning is that the one who shared with me in my eating and drinking was preparing to deal treacherously with me and entrap me ... and the direct meaning of "hath lifted up his heel against me" is: kicked me with his foot.

13.13.0.en: "Now I tell you": that is, so that you may not be offended in Me when the sufferings of the Cross begin with Judas' betraying Me, when I shall appear as a man with no strength and no power. Rather, then you will remember what I told you before, that on the one hand I am the Christ ... and on the other, that I prophesied that this would happen.

13.14.0.en: The talk here is about the sending of the disciples. Here Christ made the honor of the servant a part of His own honor, so that whoever receives the servant of Christ is as though he received the Father and the Son together. And whoever rejects the servant who is sent rejects the One who sent him, who is God Himself (see Mt 10:14; Mk 6:11; Lk 9:5).

13.15.0.en: "Troubled": this clearly indicates signs of unease on the face of Christ, as a result of His contemplating the betrayal of one of His loved ones, Judas, and the enormity of the hideousness of this sin, which made the holy nature of Christ shudder at its mere mention and at telling the disciples of it ... Christ confirmed His prophecy by saying: "Verily, verily," because He knew very well how hard it would be for the disciples to believe what He foretold, that one of them would betray Him.

13.15.1.en: Perhaps we may reflect here on what our daily sins do to the person of the Lord Jesus, or to the Holy Spirit who dwells in us ... How many times do we grieve Him every day?! And how many times do we please Him in all our life by true repentance and abandoning sin?

13.16.0.en: Astonishment, wonder and bewilderment seized all the disciples; indeed, the words of the Lord Christ were almost like a thunderbolt too incredible to believe, for even if betrayal were to come, it was far from their minds to imagine that one of them would be its source. This shows us the extent of Judas' cunning and hypocrisy, by which he deceived everyone. And when the bewilderment grew with no answer, Peter motioned to John, who was close to the bosom of Christ, to ask who it was!

13.16.1.en: "Whom Jesus loved": an expression St. John used to refer to himself, hiding his name out of humility, trusting that the reader would understand his intent. We must make clear that Christ's love had no partiality or distinction of one disciple from another; rather, according to how much a person strives to receive, Christ gives of His love. John was closer to Christ than the others, so he also enjoyed this love more than the others.

13.16.2.en: Truly, among the miracles of Christ's love for man is that everyone who loves Christ with true love feels that the Lord Christ is wholly his own possession ... Truly, how beautiful You are, O Lord.

13.17.0.en: St. John responded to the sign of Peter the Apostle and asked Christ, who instead of answering with the name of Judas used a sign, careful not to embarrass him among the disciples. And more wonderful still, the sign that Christ used, which was dipping a morsel in a dish containing a mixture of fruit juices blended with wine or vinegar and giving it to Judas, was used only as a symbol of honoring a dear guest, or the eldest son who is close to his father ... as though Christ were giving Judas a last opportunity, as one dear to Him and close to Him, as though He were saying to him: If only you would not commit this great error. But without interfering with his will.

13.18.0.en: "Satan entered into him": the conspiracy and the agreement with the chief priests had already been made (see v. 2), but the meaning of "Satan entered into him" is that Satan took firm hold of Judas' will, and he no longer had any hesitation in betraying the person of the Lord. The Lord, who searches the hearts and determines the times, knew this, and gave permission for Himself to be betrayed through the traitor, to confirm that He alone has the authority to lay down His life and to take it again.

13.19.0.en: Since Judas held the money box, the furthest the disciples' understanding of Christ's words to him reached at that time was that He was commissioning him to hasten to buy what was needed for the feast before the crowding, or to give something of the money for the service of the poor.

13.19.1.en: This teaches us not to forget the service of the poor and their needs out of our money, which is a gift of God, deposited with us in trust. So do not close your heart, beloved, to the needs of a brother of yours in Christ, in whose place you might well have been.

13.20.0.en: "Having received the sop": it was a morsel from the Passover supper, and not from the Lord's Supper and the Eucharist.

13.20.1.en: This is what our Church teaches: Judas, in whose heart evil had been kindled, rose in haste to carry out his conspiracy, and did not attend the table of the Lord's Supper with the rest of the disciples. Therefore the liturgical icon of the Lord's Supper in the Church depicts eleven disciples, and not twelve.

13.21.0.en: Here Christ begins a long discourse, which extends to the end of chapter seventeen.

13.21.1.en: "Now": that is, from the going out of Judas, the story of the glorification of the Son began. The glory meant here is the glory of His humility and of His love for mankind, in which He gave Himself even to death. It is the glory of the Son's obedience to the Father in the complete emptying of Himself. It is also the glory of the Cross, which the world does not understand, and it is a glory that precedes the glory of the Resurrection and Ascension, and the return to His true glory by sitting on His heavenly throne, which is temporarily hidden by His incarnation.

13.21.2.en: "God is glorified in Him": this means that the glory of the Son is bound to the glory of the Father. The Father is glorified by the Son, because the purpose and will of the Father are fulfilled in the redemption by the Son. And since the glory of the Father was accomplished through the Son, who continued to reveal the glory of the Father throughout His incarnation, and revealed it all the more at the time of His redemption, the Father also will reveal all the glory of the Son that belongs to Him and is hidden from the eyes of all; and this revelation begins quickly with the events of the Cross:

13.21.3.en: First: by the fulfillment in Him of all the prophecies, of which He was the subject and the hope.

13.21.4.en: Second: by the miraculous events, such as the darkness of the sky at the time of the crucifixion, the tearing of the veil of the Temple, and the coming out of many of the dead from their tombs. All of these are declarations of the glory of the Son, more than they are mere miraculous events.

13.22.0.en: "Little children": since the difficult time had come upon the disciples, Christ reveals His tender fatherly heart toward His disciples, and addresses them as "children," because of the sense in this address of the Son's reassurance at the presence and care of his father. Then He begins to refer to what is coming, and to the nearness of His separation from them, and that what He was about to go through He must pass through alone, and no one can share it with Him or follow Him in it.

13.23.0.en: Christ made love the mark that distinguishes His disciples, and everyone who follows Him among His flock, before the whole world, even without asking for a name or identity. People see the love of Christians, and so they know who they are and to whom they belong. But what is meant by calling it a new commandment, although God also commanded love in the Old Testament? What is new in the commandment of love is its dimension and depth, for it is no longer a commandment or an obligation, but a life that all Christians receive from a God who loved even unto death and gave Himself, who once bent down and washed feet, and had no rest in His body for the sake of the rest of those around Him. It is a new and unique model, which surpassed the level of love for the neighbor to the level of love for the enemy and the one who hates (Mt 5:44). It is a love that the ordinary natural man cannot reach, but only the Christian who abides in his God, and who has a living ecclesial communion through the sacraments of the Church, and especially partaking of the most honored Body and Blood of the Lord.

13.24.0.en: Peter's question about where Christ was going is an inquiry about what Christ Himself said in (v. 33), about His going to a place where no one can come. So Christ affirmed the same statement once more, showing that the first part, which concerns redemption and the way of suffering, Christ would pass through alone, and Peter, in spite of his love, could not share it or follow Christ in it. But after the Resurrection and the descent of the Holy Spirit, Peter and the rest of the disciples would follow Christ on a long road of preaching, evangelizing, endurance, and sufferings even to martyrdom. And finally, following Christ to heaven and all its glories.

13.25.0.en: Emotion and human zeal overcame Peter, so he spoke of what he did not understand, and claimed what he could not do and offer.

13.25.1.en: He did not understand that redemption, in the eternal purpose of God, could be accomplished by no one but Christ alone, and also that he could not live up to the courage that he expected in himself, and which he proclaimed with some pride: "Although all shall be offended, yet will not I" (Mk 14:29).

13.25.2.en: This teaches us not to claim for ourselves what we do not possess, and to present ourselves to the Lord Christ in humility, without boasting or false confidence in ourselves. For Christ works through the weak and the small, and resists those who are proud and great in their own eyes. And may we, my beloved brother, keep before our eyes the word of divine inspiration on the tongue of Paul the Apostle: "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me" (2 Cor 12:9).

13.26.0.en: Christ began His answer to Peter with a question of protest: "Wilt thou lay down thy life for my sake?" as though He were asking him: Do you know what you are saying?! And to show him the great difference between what he spoke and what would come from him. Christ continues His discourse with the prophecy of Peter's denial of Him, and the setting of a sign by which Peter would remember his denial of Christ, which is the crowing of the cock.

13.26.1.en: Perhaps we learn, my friend, that without God we cannot do or offer anything. But by relying on Him, and on the Holy Spirit who dwells in us, we can become Peter, who afterward offered his life with joy for the sake of Christ.

13.26.2.en: Christ comforts His disciples and promises them the Holy Spirit
